transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 14:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Simon Reeves (Hawthorn - Head of ML), Priya Nair (CTO), Liam Ortega (Infra)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on per-token economics and whether Hawthorn should go hosted -> dedicated or private. Main concerns: monthly budget cap, batching/caching opportunities, latency targets for traders, and security/compliance. Agreed to share detailed cost model and run a benchmark pilot.

Topics: pricing per-token, reserved capacity vs hosted burst, batching and KV cache impacts, quantization tradeoffs, private/VPC latencies, expected token volumes, pilot scope.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um I'm Alex from Redwood, and with me is Maya our SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:05] Simon Reeves: good, thanks. busy day but excited. we — we ran your benchmark doc last week, ps, there was a question around the token math.
[00:12] Maya Patel: cool — thanks for that. yeah we saw your notes, and wanted to use today to walk through per-token economics and the levers you have like batching, prefix caching, and if you move to Dedicated or Private how that changes unit cost.
[00:22] Priya Nair: quick context: we are a quant research team, want to deploy assistants for traders and generate embeddings for signal matching. budget is the hard constraint — we'd like to keep inference under $15k a month to start.
[00:33] Liam Ortega: and infra constraints: we run in GCP us-west, need VPC peering for private deployment, and latency target is 150ms p95 for short chat flows (<=256 tokens).
[00:42] Alex Chen: okay great; that helps. can you remind us expected volumes — approx tokens per month or QPS?
[00:47] Simon Reeves: rough numbers: about 60k prompts/day, average generation 180 tokens, so ballpark 11M tokens/day, which is ~330M tokens/month. we know that's big; initial plans are to throttle and pilot smaller but want realistic unit costs.
[01:00] Maya Patel: ok that scale is helpful. so the big levers are: model choice (open vs fine-tuned), quantization, batching (higher throughput reduces per-token), and KV/prefix caching for repeated contexts.
[01:12] Maya Patel: for hosted pricing, our public per-token rates for the large open model variants start at about $0.00008 per input/output token for standard float models — with batching and caching you can often reduce effective cost by 20-40% depending on hit rates. (note: exact numbers in the sheet Alex will send)
[01:29] Priya Nair: that starting rate would put them well above our $15k target if we used hosted naive per-token math on 330M tokens/month.
[01:36] Alex Chen: right, on naive math 330M * $0.00008 ~ $26.4k. but with caching and batching and moving to Dedicated reserved capacity we can get to lower effective unit economics. for Dedicated reserved pools we do commit pricing — typical savings versus hosted can be 30-50% depending on commit level and utilization.
[01:54] Simon Reeves: ok so can you give an example scenario? like if we commit to a 3-month reserved pool what would the per-token look like?
[02:00] Maya Patel: example: if you reserve a dedicated 2xA100-equivalent pool sized for your peak throughput and hit acceptable utilization we might price the compute at, say, $X/hour which amortizes to an effective per-token of maybe $0.00004 - $0.00006 after accounting for batching improvements. I'll put precise example numbers in the spreadsheet — the important bit is utilization.
[02:18] Liam Ortega: and what about KV caching? our workflows have repeated prompts with small variations — could that actually cut tokens significantly?
[02:24] Maya Patel: yes — prefix/KV caching is huge for trades where you have a large shared context. if you can cache the first N tokens (the expensive KV load) and subsequent calls reuse the cache, the marginal cost per call drops a lot. typical hit rates we've seen range 15-50% depending on app design.
[02:38] Simon Reeves: hmm 50% hit rate would change the math a lot. we have some shared market context that repeats across sessions so plausible.
[02:44] Priya Nair: security question: if we go Dedicated vs Private, what changes on data retention and KMS?
[02:49] Alex Chen: Dedicated keeps data logically separated and you can have longer retention options; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control — you manage KMS/HSM, audit logs stay on your side. both options can be SOC 2 compliant; Private just adds that extra isolation and control that some regulated desks require.
[03:05] Maya Patel: also performance-wise Private can reduce network hops for on-prem, but you then take on some operational overhead. for latency targets you might actually gain if you colocate.
[03:15] Liam Ortega: and is there a difference in the model variants available in Private vs Hosted? like quantized model support?
[03:20] Maya Patel: we support the same model catalog across environments; some quantization paths are more mature on host GPU drivers but we've been shipping 4-bit and 8-bit quantized runtime for both Dedicated and Private. we'll note any kernel caveats in the doc.
[03:32] Alex Chen: quick interjection — one common trap is assuming batching always helps latency. at low QPS batching can increase tail latency. so you need workload-aware batching (we have autoscaling/batching policies in the platform).
[03:44] Simon Reeves: right — traders want snappy responses, so p95 matters more than average cost. how do you balance that?
[03:50] Maya Patel: you can set per-route latency SLOs and have Smart Routing — critical routes go to low-latency capacity (smaller batch sizes), less critical analytical jobs go to high-throughput pools with larger batching. that's how you get cost savings without breaking SLOs.
[04:03] Priya Nair: our initial plan is to keep live trader flows on very low latency (p95 <=150ms) and batch embeddings/offline tasks overnight where latency isn't sensitive.
[04:12] Alex Chen: that maps well to a mixed deployment: Dedicated for live flows with reserved low-latency nodes, and either Hosted or Dedicated larger pools for embeddings. you can also route by policy.
[04:23] Simon Reeves: for the pilot, we want a real-world benchmark: run our prompt set plus typical concurrency and measure p50/p95 and cost. what's involved?
[04:30] Maya Patel: we usually ask for a sample prompt set (you provide), a small infra window where we run identical traffic against Redwood Dedicated and your in-house baseline if you want, and then we produce a cost-vs-latency report. we can do 2-3 hour runs to capture steady-state batching effects.
[04:44] Liam Ortega: we'd need an agent or access for the test — we can spin up a VPC peering for Private or give IP allowlist for Dedicated. which is faster to stand up?
[04:52] Alex Chen: Dedicated with IP allowlist is usually fastest — private VPC peering requires cloud infra team's involvement and can take a few days. for an initial benchmark Dedicated is quickest.
[04:59] Simon Reeves: ok good. pricing asks — does Redwood have a simple model for showing 'break-even' points for switching to Dedicated?
[05:06] Maya Patel: yes — our cost model spreadsheet includes columns: tokens/month, hit-rate cache, avg tokens per call, batching factor, per-hour reserved cost, and then calculated effective per-token. we'll fill that with your numbers and show break-even where reserved capacity cost becomes cheaper than hosted.
[05:21] Priya Nair: great. one more question — are there any minimum commitments? our legal team hates open-ended commitments.
[05:27] Alex Chen: we do flexible terms; Dedicated has minimums depending on pool size and commit length — typical pilots are month-to-month reserved trial or 3-month short commits. we'll include options in the sheet and Alex will flag the contract team.
[05:38] Simon Reeves: perfect. I'm also curious about model updates — like if you pin a model variant and we later want an improved quantized option, how do rollouts work without breaking performance?
[05:46] Maya Patel: we support canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies. you can pin, run A/B on a small percentage, and if latency or quality regressions show up we have automatic fallback to previous variant. our console shows per-model token breakdowns so you can monitor cost impact.
[06:00] Liam Ortega: ok curious about the numbers again — can you share an illustrative example in the call? like cached vs uncached cost with our inputs?
[06:06] Maya Patel: sure: take your avg 180 token generation. if cached hit rate 30% and batching factor yields 1.8x efficiency, effective tokens might look like 180 * (1 - 0.3) / 1.8 + cache-marginal ~ roughly 70 effective tokens per call. multiplied by your calls/day that drops total tokens by ~60% relative to naive. then multiply by hosted per-token rate to get cost. full math in sheet.
[06:29] Simon Reeves: that example helps a ton. so action items from our side: we'll send a representative prompt set, and an initial QPS profile.
[06:36] Priya Nair: and we'll confirm whether procurement can do a 3-month pilot budget of up to $20k.
[06:41] Alex Chen: great. so next step I'll send the pricing spreadsheet and a sample Dedicated config; Maya will attach the batching/caching guide and the benchmark runbook. then we schedule the 2-hour benchmark for week of the 9th — does that work?
[06:54] Simon Reeves: yep, works for us.
[06:56] Priya Nair: yes.
[06:57] Liam Ortega: ok.
[07:00] Alex Chen: good — couple of quick clarifications on compliance: we support SSO/SAML, role-based access (RBAC), SOC2 reports, and we can provide architecture docs for VPC peering for Private. any additional regs?
[07:11] Priya Nair: not now; trading desk has some internal audit but SOC2 + KMS control should be enough for initial pilot.
[07:17] Maya Patel: noted. I'll include the SOC2 attestation and our audit log export options in the packet.
[07:22] Simon Reeves: small nit — when you send the pricing, can you show both per-token and per-hour reserved cost side-by-side? makes it easier for our finance team.
[07:29] Alex Chen: yes we'll provide both and a break-even chart.
[07:33] Priya Nair: also include any hidden fees — data egress between regions, storage retention charges.
[07:38] Maya Patel: we'll call those out explicitly in the spreadsheet.
[07:42] Simon Reeves: cool. thanks everyone — this was helpful.
[07:46] Alex Chen: thanks — we'll follow up with the packet and proposed slots for the benchmark.
[07:50] Priya Nair: thanks.
[07:52] Liam Ortega: thanks, bye.
